content.value: Criminality comes from anywhere.

Crime is not a defect of certain people in certain places. It is what any population does when the legitimate frontier for meeting a need drifts out of reach while an illegitimate point sits nearby — and whether people come back is decided by a sanction curve with two cliffs.

items.label: job callbacks lost to a record alone¹
less reoffending, caused by humane prisons³

content.value: Every method is a point; the points form a frontier

Start with a deliberately mundane experiment: hold one goal fixed — growing a plant at home — and walk its constraints. Each tab below is one position in the money × effort space; watch what squeezing does.
No constraints.

The textbook method: proper equipment, proper stages, proper schedule. Every failure mode is deleted by some purchased component; effort and money are both spent freely. This is the point everyone imagines is
the
method. It's just the least constrained one.
The improvised version.
Scavenged containers, window light, household substitutes. Capital is replaced by cleverness — and by
accepted failure modes
the equipment would have deleted. The method survives; the reliability is what got sold.
The capitalized version.

Automation and better inputs delete failure modes one by one. Effort is roughly the integral of failure-mode correction over time — which is why money and effort keep converging on the same purchases.
The regime change.

Squeeze effort hard enough and the smooth trade-off breaks: no tuned middle version exists any more. You either buy a machine that does everything, or plant outdoors and accept a lottery. A hard constraint produces a
qualitatively different
solution — not a smaller version of the old one.

items.label: LESSON 1
items.text: For any budget of money, effort, skill and risk there is a nearby viable point.

items.label: LESSON 2
items.lead: The frontier is dense and improvisable.
items.text: Delete a point and its neighbours regenerate — suppression fights geometry.

items.label: LESSON 3
items.text: Push a constraint hard enough and you get a different solution, not a gradient.

content.value: Where crime comes from
Now invert the picture. People have needs — income, status, security, belonging. Legitimate methods for meeting those needs also form a frontier, and that frontier is not equally reachable.

blocks.cite: Robert K. Merton, “Social Structure and Anomie”, 1938

content.value: It is only when a system of cultural values extols, virtually above all else, certain common symbols of success for the population at large while its social structure rigorously restricts or completely eliminates access to approved modes of acquiring these symbols for a considerable part of the same population that antisocial behavior ensues on a considerable scale.

Crime emerges wherever a legitimate method for meeting a need is out of reach while an illegitimate point is within reach. Everyone, everywhere, has some reachable illicit point — so no geography or class is immune. What varies is which point is reachable.
Which point is reachable is set by three axes — and each axis is a different kind of gate:

Fixes the reachable region of the legitimate frontier. Where legal income routes are blocked or slow, the relative price of the nearest illicit point drops. Becker's expected-utility layer prices the choice.

Criminal methods are learned socially (Sutherland); illegitimate opportunity is also unevenly distributed (Cloward & Ohlin). You cannot traffic weapons without a trafficking network, however strained you are.
Self-control, risk tolerance, violence tolerance (Gottfredson & Hirschi). Heavier rungs cost variance — exposure to prison and death — not money. Personality decides whether that currency is payable.
Gated markets, not a slippery slope

The severity ladder — cultivation, dealing, organized distribution, trafficking and enforcement — looks like a slope but behaves like the corners of the constraint space: every transition is a regime change with a different binding constraint, and every gate filters people out.

When leaving crime costs more than staying

Here is the part the ladder alone misses: for someone deep enough in, the incentives to stay in crime are stronger than anyone's incentives to leave. That is not a metaphor — it is a measurable structure with three interlocking mechanisms.

items.label: MECHANISM 1
items.lead: Punishment past a point brands rather than deters.
items.text: The label, not just the act, produces the next offence: the record halves job callbacks¹; formally processing a first juvenile offence increases reoffending vs diversion⁴; first arrests trigger secondary sanctioning — arrests beget arrests through the system's own memory.

items.label: MECHANISM 2
items.lead: The more a person has lost, the less any threat bites.
items.text: Deterrence runs on stakes. Strip job, housing, family and standing, and the state has spent its leverage; sanctions felt as unfair on the poorly bonded produce defiant pride, not compliance⁵ — and under three-strikes maximums the marginal price of violence hits zero⁶.

items.label: MECHANISM 3
items.lead: Exclusion cuts the one lifeline that ends criminal careers.
items.text: Half a century of the Glueck cohort says desistance rides on belonging: marriage, work, service⁷. Stigmatizing shame hands the rejected to the one community still selling status — the subculture⁸.

blocks.title: Figure 3 — Callback rate, matched entry-level applicants (Pager 2003)¹

content.value: Same résumés, same demeanor — the record alone halves consideration, and a white applicant with a record out-polls a Black applicant without one.

Punishment past the sweet spot does not just fail to deter — it manufactures the very persistence it claims to fight: it deletes stakes, closes exits, and hands the excluded to the one community still offering membership.
No punishment, and the leeches inherit the earth

If over-punishment traps individuals, under-punishment dissolves the commons — one of the most replicated results in experimental economics⁹. In repeated public-goods games, cooperation without a sanctioning option decays toward zero: most people are
conditional
cooperators, so every unpunished free rider licenses the next defection. When most people leech, everyone leeches.

blocks.caption: Figure 4 — The two regimes of the public-goods game (stylized from Fehr & Gächter 2000⁹). Same people, same stakes; the only difference is whether peers can sanction. Remarkably, people PAY their own money to punish leeches who never harmed them — the appetite for punishment is the evolved immune system of cooperation.

content.value: Between the two cliffs

blocks.caption: Figure 5 — The sanction curve is a U, not a line.

content.value: No rules → confusion about right and wrong → exploitation of the confusion without mercy → imitation of the exploiters. The cascade is fast, and it is not hypothetical: it is the no-sanction arm of figure 4.

Stigma, defiance, nothing left to lose. Punishment past the mark deletes stakes, closes exits, severs belonging — and manufactures exactly the persistence it claims to fight. It is the record bar of figure 3.

blocks.title: The right cliff — the branding trap

content.value: The empirical literature is unusually consistent about what the valley looks like — four findings, each with its own instrument:
Certainty beats severity.
Five decades of deterrence research reach one headline conclusion: the
certainty
of apprehension deters;
severity
at the margin does not¹⁰. Lengthy sentences and mandatory minimums cannot be justified on deterrence grounds. The offender's brain asks “will I get caught?”, not “what is the statutory maximum?”

blocks.title: Figure 6 — HOPE vs probation-as-usual, Hawaii randomized trial (%)²

content.value: Swift-certain-mild works in the field.
HOPE flipped the usual regime: every violation drew an immediate, guaranteed sanction of a few
days
— and every outcome improved while total punishment administered went
down
. Milder punishment, delivered reliably, out-deterred harsher punishment delivered as a lottery.

blocks.title: Figure 7 — Share of released prisoners who reoffend (%)

content.value: Reintegration is not softness; it is the mechanism.
Because Norwegian criminal cases are as-good-as-randomly assigned to judges of differing strictness, the judge-lottery design measures what prison itself
causes
: in a system built around education, training and open prisons, incarceration
reduced

five-year reoffending by 29 percentage points and pushed unemployed offenders into work³. Prison, done reintegratively, rehabilitates — “nothing works” is false. The disintegrative version is what manufactures recidivists.

blocks.cite: John Braithwaite, Crime, Shame and Reintegration, 1989⁸

content.value: The best place to see reintegrative shaming at work is the loving family… Family life teaches us that shaming and punishment are possible while maintaining bonds of respect.
And the sanction must feel fair.

Sanctions experienced as unfair and stigmatizing, landing on the poorly bonded, produce more crime, not less⁵. Procedural justice — being heard, respected, rules applied evenly — is a crime-reduction technology. Braithwaite's formula compresses the whole valley into one sentence:
condemn the act, never the person, and follow every degradation ceremony with a ceremony that decertifies the deviance.

(fig. 4) is stylized from the published round means, not digitized data.
HOPE
(fig. 6): later multi-site replications were weaker than the original trial — the swift-certain-fair family still outperforms, but effect sizes vary with implementation fidelity.
Norway vs U.S.

(fig. 7): reconviction vs rearrest — different measures; read as regimes, not a controlled comparison; the honest comparison is each system against its own history (Norway's own 2-year rate fell from the 60–70% range to ~20% after its 1990s reforms). Gauge digits round to whole percent; the exact U.S. 5-year figure is 76.6%.

content.value: Move the frontiers, shape the curve

Put the two halves together and the policy geometry falls out. The first half showed method frontiers are dense and regenerating — suppressing points fights geometry itself. The second half showed the sanction curve is a U. Together they yield seven design rules:
Every krone moved from sentence-length to detection probability buys deterrence; the reverse buys prison beds and branded people.
HOPE's days-not-months regime is the template: consequences close enough to the act to teach, small enough to leave stakes standing.

steps.title: Keep sanctions swift, mild and utterly predictable

content.value: Proportionality is not sentimentality — a price gradient is what stops a burglar from becoming a killer of witnesses. Never price the maximum into the middle of the ladder.

Reintegrative shame condemns the act and keeps membership; stigma hands the person to the subculture. Expunge stale records; audit every collateral consequence that closes the labour-market door figure 3 measured.

steps.title: Punish inside the circle, not out of it

content.value: Desistance rides on work, family and belonging. Prison time that ends without a job, a home and a network is a subscription renewal, not a sentence served.
Jobs, training and credit put legal points within more budgets; regulated legalization moves whole frontier segments out of criminal space entirely.

steps.title: Raise the legitimate frontier; relocate what you can off the illicit map

content.value: The left cliff is real: unpunished free-riding cascades. The valley is not the absence of consequences — it is consequences engineered to be cheap, certain, fair and survivable.

steps.title: Never confuse the valley with zero

content.value: A person deep in criminality is not beyond incentives — they are responding perfectly to the incentives we built. The system that branded them, stripped their stakes and severed their belonging is getting exactly the behaviour it pays for.

Barkpark Papers · essay

Criminality comes from anywhere.

Crime is not a defect of certain people in certain places. It is what any population does when the legitimate frontier for meeting a need drifts out of reach while an illegitimate point sits nearby — and whether people come back is decided by a sanction curve with two cliffs.

01 · The frontier walk

Every method is a point; the points form a frontier

Start with a deliberately mundane experiment: hold one goal fixed — growing a plant at home — and walk its constraints. Each tab below is one position in the money × effort space; watch what squeezing does.

№1 · Baseline

No constraints. The textbook method: proper equipment, proper stages, proper schedule. Every failure mode is deleted by some purchased component; effort and money are both spent freely. This is the point everyone imagines is the method. It's just the least constrained one.

№2 · Money ↓

The improvised version. Scavenged containers, window light, household substitutes. Capital is replaced by cleverness — and by accepted failure modes the equipment would have deleted. The method survives; the reliability is what got sold.

№3 · Effort ↓

The capitalized version. Automation and better inputs delete failure modes one by one. Effort is roughly the integral of failure-mode correction over time — which is why money and effort keep converging on the same purchases.

№4 · The extreme

The regime change. Squeeze effort hard enough and the smooth trade-off breaks: no tuned middle version exists any more. You either buy a machine that does everything, or plant outdoors and accept a lottery. A hard constraint produces a qualitatively different solution — not a smaller version of the old one.

LESSON 1Methods form a Pareto frontier. For any budget of money, effort, skill and risk there is a nearby viable point.
LESSON 2The frontier is dense and improvisable. Delete a point and its neighbours regenerate — suppression fights geometry.
LESSON 3Extremes produce regime changes. Push a constraint hard enough and you get a different solution, not a gradient.

02 · The inversion

Where crime comes from

Now invert the picture. People have needs — income, status, security, belonging. Legitimate methods for meeting those needs also form a frontier, and that frontier is not equally reachable.

It is only when a system of cultural values extols, virtually above all else, certain common symbols of success for the population at large while its social structure rigorously restricts or completely eliminates access to approved modes of acquiring these symbols for a considerable part of the same population that antisocial behavior ensues on a considerable scale.— Robert K. Merton, “Social Structure and Anomie”, 1938

Crime emerges wherever a legitimate method for meeting a need is out of reach while an illegitimate point is within reach. Everyone, everywhere, has some reachable illicit point — so no geography or class is immune. What varies is which point is reachable.

Which point is reachable is set by three axes — and each axis is a different kind of gate:

Economics — what is affordable
Fixes the reachable region of the legitimate frontier. Where legal income routes are blocked or slow, the relative price of the nearest illicit point drops. Becker's expected-utility layer prices the choice.
Culture — what is visible
Criminal methods are learned socially (Sutherland); illegitimate opportunity is also unevenly distributed (Cloward & Ohlin). You cannot traffic weapons without a trafficking network, however strained you are.
Personality — what variance is payable
Self-control, risk tolerance, violence tolerance (Gottfredson & Hirschi). Heavier rungs cost variance — exposure to prison and death — not money. Personality decides whether that currency is payable.

03 · The ladder

Gated markets, not a slippery slope

The severity ladder — cultivation, dealing, organized distribution, trafficking and enforcement — looks like a slope but behaves like the corners of the constraint space: every transition is a regime change with a different binding constraint, and every gate filters people out.

04 · The trap

When leaving crime costs more than staying

Here is the part the ladder alone misses: for someone deep enough in, the incentives to stay in crime are stronger than anyone's incentives to leave. That is not a metaphor — it is a measurable structure with three interlocking mechanisms.

MECHANISM 1Punishment past a point brands rather than deters. The label, not just the act, produces the next offence: the record halves job callbacks¹; formally processing a first juvenile offence increases reoffending vs diversion⁴; first arrests trigger secondary sanctioning — arrests beget arrests through the system's own memory.
MECHANISM 2The more a person has lost, the less any threat bites. Deterrence runs on stakes. Strip job, housing, family and standing, and the state has spent its leverage; sanctions felt as unfair on the poorly bonded produce defiant pride, not compliance⁵ — and under three-strikes maximums the marginal price of violence hits zero⁶.
MECHANISM 3Exclusion cuts the one lifeline that ends criminal careers. Half a century of the Glueck cohort says desistance rides on belonging: marriage, work, service⁷. Stigmatizing shame hands the rejected to the one community still selling status — the subculture⁸.

Punishment past the sweet spot does not just fail to deter — it manufactures the very persistence it claims to fight: it deletes stakes, closes exits, and hands the excluded to the one community still offering membership.

05 · The opposite cliff

No punishment, and the leeches inherit the earth

If over-punishment traps individuals, under-punishment dissolves the commons — one of the most replicated results in experimental economics⁹. In repeated public-goods games, cooperation without a sanctioning option decays toward zero: most people are conditional cooperators, so every unpunished free rider licenses the next defection. When most people leech, everyone leeches.

Figure 4 — The two regimes of the public-goods game (stylized from Fehr & Gächter 2000⁹). Same people, same stakes; the only difference is whether peers can sanction. Remarkably, people PAY their own money to punish leeches who never harmed them — the appetite for punishment is the evolved immune system of cooperation.

06 · The sweet spot

Between the two cliffs

Figure 5 — The sanction curve is a U, not a line.

No rules → confusion about right and wrong → exploitation of the confusion without mercy → imitation of the exploiters. The cascade is fast, and it is not hypothetical: it is the no-sanction arm of figure 4.
The right cliff — the branding trap
Stigma, defiance, nothing left to lose. Punishment past the mark deletes stakes, closes exits, severs belonging — and manufactures exactly the persistence it claims to fight. It is the record bar of figure 3.

Certainty beats severity. Five decades of deterrence research reach one headline conclusion: the certainty of apprehension deters; severity at the margin does not¹⁰. Lengthy sentences and mandatory minimums cannot be justified on deterrence grounds. The offender's brain asks “will I get caught?”, not “what is the statutory maximum?”

Reintegration is not softness; it is the mechanism. And the sanction must feel fair. Sanctions experienced as unfair and stigmatizing, landing on the poorly bonded, produce more crime, not less⁵. Procedural justice — being heard, respected, rules applied evenly — is a crime-reduction technology. Braithwaite's formula compresses the whole valley into one sentence: condemn the act, never the person, and follow every degradation ceremony with a ceremony that decertifies the deviance.

Fehr & Gächter series (fig. 4) is stylized from the published round means, not digitized data. HOPE (fig. 6): later multi-site replications were weaker than the original trial — the swift-certain-fair family still outperforms, but effect sizes vary with implementation fidelity. Gauge digits round to whole percent; the exact U.S. 5-year figure is 76.6%.

07 · Design rules

Move the frontiers, shape the curve

Put the two halves together and the policy geometry falls out. The first half showed method frontiers are dense and regenerating — suppressing points fights geometry itself. The second half showed the sanction curve is a U. Together they yield seven design rules:

  1. Spend on certainty, not severity

    Every krone moved from sentence-length to detection probability buys deterrence; the reverse buys prison beds and branded people.

  2. Keep sanctions swift, mild and utterly predictable

    HOPE's days-not-months regime is the template: consequences close enough to the act to teach, small enough to leave stakes standing.

  3. Preserve marginal deterrence

    Proportionality is not sentimentality — a price gradient is what stops a burglar from becoming a killer of witnesses. Never price the maximum into the middle of the ladder.

  4. Punish inside the circle, not out of it

    Reintegrative shame condemns the act and keeps membership; stigma hands the person to the subculture. Expunge stale records; audit every collateral consequence that closes the labour-market door figure 3 measured.

  5. Build exits at every gate

    Desistance rides on work, family and belonging. Prison time that ends without a job, a home and a network is a subscription renewal, not a sentence served.

  6. Raise the legitimate frontier; relocate what you can off the illicit map

    Jobs, training and credit put legal points within more budgets; regulated legalization moves whole frontier segments out of criminal space entirely.

  7. Never confuse the valley with zero

    The left cliff is real: unpunished free-riding cascades. The valley is not the absence of consequences — it is consequences engineered to be cheap, certain, fair and survivable.

A person deep in criminality is not beyond incentives — they are responding perfectly to the incentives we built. The system that branded them, stripped their stakes and severed their belonging is getting exactly the behaviour it pays for.

Criminality comes from anywhere.

Crime is not a defect of certain people in certain places. It is what any population does when the legitimate frontier for meeting a need drifts out of reach while an illegitimate point sits nearby — and whether people come back is decided by a sanction curve with two cliffs.

01 · The frontier walk

Every method is a point; the points form a frontier

No constraints. The textbook method: proper equipment, proper stages, proper schedule. Every failure mode is deleted by some purchased component; effort and money are both spent freely. This is the point everyone imagines is the method. It's just the least constrained one.

The improvised version. Scavenged containers, window light, household substitutes. Capital is replaced by cleverness — and by accepted failure modes the equipment would have deleted. The method survives; the reliability is what got sold.

The capitalized version. Automation and better inputs delete failure modes one by one. Effort is roughly the integral of failure-mode correction over time — which is why money and effort keep converging on the same purchases.

The regime change. Squeeze effort hard enough and the smooth trade-off breaks: no tuned middle version exists any more. You either buy a machine that does everything, or plant outdoors and accept a lottery. A hard constraint produces a qualitatively different solution — not a smaller version of the old one.

LESSON 1
Methods form a Pareto frontier. For any budget of money, effort, skill and risk there is a nearby viable point.
LESSON 2
The frontier is dense and improvisable. Delete a point and its neighbours regenerate — suppression fights geometry.
LESSON 3
Extremes produce regime changes. Push a constraint hard enough and you get a different solution, not a gradient.

Now invert the picture. People have needs — income, status, security, belonging. Legitimate methods for meeting those needs also form a frontier, and that frontier is not equally reachable.

Robert K. Merton, “Social Structure and Anomie”, 1938

Personality — what variance is payable Self-control, risk tolerance, violence tolerance (Gottfredson & Hirschi). Heavier rungs cost variance — exposure to prison and death — not money. Personality decides whether that currency is payable.
